summary: Adds an optional OSPF extension for multi-access networks that gives each router a metric to the network and a separate metric from the network. The router-to-router cost is the sum. It updates RFC 2328.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one price for each trip, the cost of getting onto a bus and the cost of getting off are listed separately and added. That is fairer for busy shared networks.

subtitle: An OSPF extension that splits a shared network's cost into a to-network part and a from-network part.

tldr.problem: On some broadcast networks, such as a satellite radio network, each router can be reached with a different metric, and listing individual metrics to every neighbor makes Router-LSAs large and update-heavy.
tldr.mechanism: Each router advertises its normal metric to the network plus a new network-to-router metric. The router-to-router metric is the sum of the sender's to-network part and the receiver's from-network part.
tldr.outcome: Router-LSAs are much smaller, and when one router's link quality changes only that router needs to update its LSA. The extension is optional and updates RFC 2328.

today: RFC 8042 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2016 that updates RFC 2328. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem on Shared Networks
sections.content:
In OSPF, a Network-LSA lists all routers on a broadcast network, and each router has a link in its Router-LSA with a metric to the network. The Network-LSA entries carry no metric, because the base protocol assumes that from one router every other router can be reached with the same metric.

On some broadcast networks that is not true. RFC 6845 handles this with a hybrid interface type where no Network-LSA is advertised and Router-LSAs contain point-to-point links with individual metrics to all routers. That works when metrics between pairs are really independent, as in VPLS networks.

For other networks it scales badly. In a satellite radio network with fixed and mobile ground terminals, one terminal moving to a place with weak communication changes the metric to it from every other router and from it to every other router. Every router must then update its large Router-LSA, and many fast-moving terminals could inhibit network scaling.
sections.plainLanguage: If one kid on a walkie-talkie game walks far away, everyone would have to rewrite their whole list of how well they can hear every other kid. That is a lot of rewriting.

sections.title: Splitting the Metric in Two
sections.content:
The RFC observes that when one terminal's capability changes, the metric to it and from it change in a similar way for everybody. So the metric is broken into two parts: the metric to the satellite and the metric from the satellite. The metric from terminal R1 to R2 is the sum of R1 to the satellite and the satellite to R2.

The network is then treated as a regular broadcast network rather than a hybrid interface. A router no longer lists a metric to each neighbor. It advertises the normal Router-to-Network metric plus an additional Network-to-Router metric for itself, and individual Router-to-Router metrics are computed from those.

The Router-LSA shrinks, and when one router's capability changes only that router updates its LSA. The satellite is only a relay at layer 2 and does not need to run any layer-3 protocol, so the metric is described generally as to and from the "network".
sections.plainLanguage: Each kid just announces how well they can send to the middle and how well they can hear from the middle. Add one kid's sending to another's hearing and you know how well they can talk.

sections.title: Interface Parameters and Advertising
sections.content:
Router interface parameters get two additions. Two-part metric is TRUE when the interface connects to a multi-access network using a two-part metric, and all routers on that network SHOULD be configured the same way. Interface input cost is the link-state metric from the network to this router. It defaults to the interface output cost and may be configured or adjusted dynamically to differ from it.

In OSPFv2 the network-to-router metric is carried in a new Network-to-Router Metric Sub-TLV, type 4, inside an OSPF Extended Link TLV in an Extended-Link Opaque LSA. Its value is 4 bytes: an MT-ID, a zero byte and a 16-bit MT Metric. There can be one such sub-TLV per topology, each with a unique MT-ID. It MUST ONLY appear for Link Type 2 (link to transit network) and is ignored for other link types.

A matching Traffic Engineering Network-to-Router Metric Sub-TLV, type 35, is defined for Type 2 Link TLVs in TE LSAs, and MUST appear at most once in such a Link TLV. The OSPFv3 encoding is left to a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router writes down a small note saying how well it hears from the middle, in a special spot that only shared-network links are allowed to use.

sections.title: SPF Calculation and Stub Routers
sections.content:
The shortest-path calculation in RFC 2328 changes in one place. When the vertex V for a Network-LSA has just joined the tree and an adjacent router W is being added to the candidate list, the cost from V to W is taken from W's Network-to-Router Metric Sub-TLV for the matching topology. If W has no such sub-TLV, the cost is 0. The normal cost to reach V is already counted, so the sum gives the two-part metric.

For stub router behavior (RFC 6987), a router with two-part-metric interfaces sets only the Router-to-Network metric in its Router-LSA links to MaxLinkMetric. The RFC says this is fully backward compatible and behaves as RFC 6987 describes.
sections.plainLanguage: To price a trip, you add the cost to get to the middle and then the cost the other kid listed for getting from the middle. If they listed nothing, that part is free.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Because the SPF procedure changes, every router in an area containing one or more two-part metric networks MUST support the extension. To guarantee that, each supporting router advertises a Router Information LSA with a Router Functional Capabilities TLV that sets bit 6, Two-Part Metric support. If a router sees a reachable Router-LSA without a companion RI LSA that has the bit set, all routers MUST recalculate routes ignoring every network-to-router cost.

IANA added the capability bit (6), the Network-to-Router Metric Sub-TLV (4) and the Network-to-Router TE Metric Sub-TLV (35) to their registries. The security section is a single statement: the document introduces no new security risks, and the existing OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 considerations apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the neighborhood has to know the new pricing rule. If even one router has not said it knows, everybody goes back to the old way.
